system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 3: Pentatonic Scale

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 3 — Pentatonic Scale

_Pages 108-139._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Pentatonic scale definition

> The pentatonic scale has .ive notes as the name suggests (penta meaning .ive, therefore,
> pentatonic means .ive notes). It is one of the most used scales in the music history. We
> have 2 types of pentatonic scales:

**Significance (p. 108).** Defines pentatonic scale, etymology, and the two-type framework.

## Major/minor pentatonic chord identity

> The major pentatonic scale creates a major 6th chord (C, E, G, A), and the minor pentatonic
> scale creates a minor 7th chord (A, C, E, G). So, for now we have the chords: C6 and Cm7.
> However, if we change the key of the minor pentatonic from Cm to Am, we would have the
> same scale and the same chord, because C6 is an inverted Am7 (1st inversion). See below:

**Significance (p. 108).** Harmonic identity of pentatonics; C6 and Am7 are same notes.

## Relative major/minor pentatonic relationship

> With all that background, we could say that there is a relative major/minor relationship
> between both pentatonic scales:
>
> • C6       →     Am7 (relative minor chord of C6)
>
> • Am7 →           C6 (relative major chord of Am7)
>
> Although both pentatonic scales contain the same notes, it is extremely important to
> visualize them separately (major and minor), because we will use them to split the guitar
> fretboard into 5 zones. So depending where we are on the freatboard we will use one or the
> other.

**Significance (p. 108).** Core rule: visualize major and minor pentatonics separately to navigate 5-zone fretboard.

## 5-zone system introduction

> Just like we did with the Ionian and Aeolian scales, let’s use the 5 vertical zones for
> pentatonic scales using the guide chords that cover the 5 vertical zones of the guitar
> fretboard. However, some of these chords have been changed to better @it the scales
> presented. This is not a rule. We could use the same chords we learned before, because they
> are only to guide us into the 5 zones, nothing else.

**Significance (p. 110).** Guide chords are navigational aids only, not harmonic rules.

## Two-notes-per-string vertical playing

> Attention:
> All the examples of pentatonic scales work perfectly when played vertically because they
> can be played using two notes per string. However, we will learn other possibilities of how
> to approach them over the guitar fretboard.

**Significance (p. 110).** Two-notes-per-string structural rule for vertical pentatonic fingerings.

## Zone connection picking problem

> Although the pentatonic connections with alternate picking work perfectly when we use
> the 1st or 6th string to change from one zone to another, we can also do this by using other

**Significance (p. 114).** Safe zone changes happen on 1st or 6th string; other strings need adjustment.

## Skipping zones to preserve hand connection

> If we are in the 1st zone going from low to high, and we want to move to another zone, we
> must skip the 2nd zone thus going to the 3rd zone. This might look difGicult, but actually it
> is much easier, otherwise the connection between both hands would be lost.

**Significance (p. 114).** Concrete rule: skip a zone to preserve hand sync.

## Practicing only preferred patterns

> It is important to understand that among the many possibilities of Gingering and picking
> we can Gind, we do not have to study all of them, only the ones we like the most, and feel
> the most comfortable with.

**Significance (p. 114).** Selective-study practice rule.

## Non-standard fingering when changing zones

> Notice that when we change from one zone to another we have a non common type of
> Dingering (4, 1, 4, 1, 4, 1 and 4, 1), which might look odd or wrong, but it works very well in
> this case.

**Significance (p. 118).** Validates finger 4/1 alternation for zone transitions.

## Simple pentatonic patterns and rhythmic cells

> After learning the pentatonic scale, it is time to memorize some simple patterns using it.

**Significance (p. 120).** Compositional trick: pair even melodies with odd rhythmic cells (or vice versa).

## Pattern note order rule

> Note: Remember that the order of the notes is always the same, the only thing that changes
> is the rhythm, otherwise we would be changing the melodic pattern.

**Significance (p. 120).** Invariant: pitch sequence fixed, only rhythm changes.
